title: NeuroAI: Brain Principles in Computing
tagline: A computing-oriented neuroscience track: neural coding, biophysical neuron models, spiking-network simulation with Brian2, and an honest synthesis of what brains and AI share — 120 hours. No medical content.

domains.name: NeuroAI: Brain Principles in Computing
domains.summary: Brain principles for computing people: neural coding, leaky integrate-and-fire and Hodgkin-Huxley models, Hebbian and STDP plasticity, Hopfield networks, spiking-network simulation with NEURON and Brian2, and an honest NeuroAI synthesis — labeled analogies, predictive coding, neuromorphic hardware, and the open backprop question. Independent study; confers no certificate. No medical content.

scenarios.title: Rate or spike?
scenarios.situation: A team records from a sensory neuron population and debates the code. One side argues mean firing rate over a 500 ms window captures everything the downstream area could use; the other insists precise spike timing carries extra information. The recordings show reliable millisecond-scale spike patterns across trials.
scenarios.prompt: How should a computing-oriented student frame this debate?
choices: Keep both hypotheses: rate coding (mean spike count, the classical Adrian view) is real and sufficient for many signals, but temporal codes — spike timing, latency, synchrony — carry information that averaging destroys, and mechanisms like STDP are explicitly timing-sensitive. The code question is empirical, not ideological.
Rate coding is the whole story: timing is always noise.
Temporal coding is the whole story: rates are obsolete.
Whichever is simpler to simulate is the correct code.
scenarios.why: The nervous system demonstrably uses both: firing rates encode stimulus intensity in many pathways, while phenomena like spike-timing-dependent plasticity and precise first-spike latencies prove downstream machinery reads timing. For computing, the lesson is architectural — your model must represent whichever code the task's mechanism actually uses.
scenarios.hint: STDP strengthens a synapse based on the relative timing of two spikes — could a pure rate code even express that rule?

scenarios.title: The silent neuron
scenarios.situation: A student implements a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Python: membrane potential integrates the input current, leaks toward rest, and should spike at threshold. The simulation runs 100 ms and the neuron never spikes, though the equations look right.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic way to debug it?
choices: Check the drive against the threshold: compute the steady-state voltage the input current would produce (V_inf = V_rest + R_m * I) and confirm it exceeds threshold — if not, the neuron is below rheobase and can never spike. Then check the leak: an excessive leak time-constant or too-high threshold has the same silencing effect. Diagnose parameters before blaming the integrator.
Halve the time step: dt is always the problem.
Add noise to the input: neurons need noise to spike.
Increase the simulation time to 10 seconds: it just needs longer.
scenarios.why: LIF dynamics have a closed-form steady state, so 'never spikes' is usually a parameter fact, not a code bug: rheobase — the minimum sustained current that drives V to threshold — is the first number to compute. This habit (steady-state analysis before longer runs) transfers to every dynamical model you will simulate.
scenarios.hint: If the leak pulls the voltage down faster than the current pushes it up, what is the highest voltage the neuron can ever reach — and is it above threshold?

scenarios.title: Hebb explodes
scenarios.situation: A student codes pure Hebbian plasticity — strengthen the synapse whenever pre fires before post — in a small recurrent network. Within seconds of simulated time every weight saturates at its maximum and all neurons fire constantly. The student concludes Hebb's rule is wrong.
choices: Unconstrained Hebbian learning is unstable by construction: positive feedback (stronger synapse → more correlated firing → stronger synapse) drives runaway growth. Biology and stable models add constraints — weight normalization, bounds, decay, or rules like Oja's and BCM with homeostatic terms. Hebb identified the correlation principle; stability requires the rest of the machinery.
Hebb's rule is wrong: discard it.
Lower the learning rate: that alone stabilizes Hebbian growth.
Remove recurrence: feedforward Hebbian networks are stable.
scenarios.why: Positive feedback without a counterforce diverges — this is dynamics, not a bug in the idea. Real synapses face normalization (total synaptic weight is regulated), and theoretical neuroscience answered with Oja's rule (which adds a forgetting term yielding principal components) and BCM (sliding threshold for stability). The exploding simulation is actually the correct result for the unconstrained rule.
scenarios.hint: If every 'fire together, wire together' event makes the next co-firing more likely, what stops the weights — and what did your simulation include as a stop?

scenarios.title: Fifty patterns, one hundred neurons
scenarios.situation: A team builds a Hopfield network with 100 binary neurons and stores 50 random patterns with the Hebbian outer-product rule. Retrieval from partial cues returns garbage — spurious mixtures instead of clean patterns. They assume the update code is broken.
choices: They exceeded capacity: a Hopfield net of N neurons reliably stores only about 0.14N random patterns (roughly 14 for N=100). Beyond that, cross-talk between stored patterns creates spurious attractors — the 'garbage' is the network correctly converging to minima the overloaded weight matrix created.
The asynchronous update order is wrong: update order causes spurious states.
The energy function has a sign error: check the code again.
Hopfield networks cannot store random patterns at all: use correlated ones.
scenarios.why: The ~0.14N capacity result (Amit, Gutfreund and Sompolinsky) is one of the field's classic calculations: each stored pattern contributes noise to every other pattern's recall. The garbage outputs are not a code bug — they are the predicted behavior of an overloaded associative memory, which is exactly why the scenario is diagnostic.
scenarios.hint: Fifty patterns into 100 neurons is 0.5 patterns per neuron — how does that compare to the known capacity scaling, and what does overload predict?

scenarios.title: Attention is not attention
scenarios.situation: A blog post claims 'transformers work because attention is how the brain works.' A student asks whether transformer self-attention and biological attention are the same mechanism, and whether the analogy justifies brain-inspired architecture claims.
choices: Name the shared function and the different mechanisms: both select and route information, but transformer attention is a differentiable softmax weighting over key-query similarities computed in parallel, while biological attention involves neuromodulatory gating, thalamocortical routing, and selective enhancement across recurrent circuits. The analogy is real at the functional level and false at the mechanistic level — label which level every claim sits on.
They are the same mechanism: the analogy is literal.
They are completely unrelated: the shared word is a coincidence.
Biological attention is just softmax with noise: implement it directly.
scenarios.why: This is the course's central discipline: analogies between AI and brains must carry their level labels. Functional similarity (selection, routing, prioritization) can inspire architectures; mechanistic claims require evidence about actual neural circuits. Collapsing the two levels is how honest inspiration becomes hype.
scenarios.hint: If you had to defend the analogy to a neuroscientist, which level — what it computes, or how the tissue implements it — could you actually defend?

scenarios.title: Does the brain do backprop?
scenarios.situation: A team member states as fact that 'the brain must do backpropagation because deep learning works.' Another counters that backprop is biologically impossible, case closed. The team looks to you for the research-literate position.
choices: It is open research, not settled syllabus: standard backprop needs weight symmetry (feedback weights mirroring feedforward weights — the weight-transport problem) with no clear biological implementation, but alternatives exist — feedback alignment shows random feedback weights can still teach, and predictive-coding circuits can approximate gradient descent. Report the debate, not a verdict.
The brain definitely does backprop: deep learning proves it.
Backprop is biologically impossible: the case is closed.
The question is irrelevant to computing: ignore biology entirely.
scenarios.why: The weight-transport problem is the sharp core of the debate: synapses are unidirectional, so symmetric feedback is not observed. But 'not standard backprop' is not 'no gradient-like learning' — feedback alignment (Lillicrap et al., 2016) and predictive coding (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Friston) keep the question genuinely open. Teaching a verdict either way would be the invented fact this course refuses.
scenarios.hint: What specific mechanism of standard backprop lacks a biological counterpart — and does that rule out every gradient-like alternative?

lessons.title: NeuroAI: Brain Principles in Computing — Core concepts
concepts: Neural coding is the representation question: rate codes (spike counts, the classical Adrian view) versus temporal codes (timing, latency, synchrony). The code your model assumes decides which mechanisms it can even express — STDP is meaningless in a pure rate model.

The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron is the workhorse abstraction: integrate input, leak toward rest, spike at threshold, reset. Its steady state (V_rest + R_m*I) tells you before any simulation whether a neuron can ever fire — rheobase first, code second.

Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) modeled the squid giant axon's action potential with voltage-gated sodium and potassium conductances (gating variables m, h, n) — the landmark that biophysics can be written as differential equations, recognized with the 1963 Nobel Prize.

Plasticity rules are correlation detectors with stability problems: Hebb (1949, 'fire together, wire together'), STDP (pre-before-post within tens of milliseconds strengthens; the reverse weakens — Bi & Poo 1998), and the homeostatic machinery (Oja, BCM) that keeps correlation learning from exploding.

Hopfield networks (1982) made memory an energy landscape: stored patterns are attractors of a recurrent dynamics, retrievable from partial cues, with capacity near 0.14N — the bridge where AI architectures and statistical physics of neural systems meet.

NeuroAI synthesis demands labeled analogies: transformer attention shares function (selection) with biological attention but not mechanism; predictive coding frames cortex as hierarchical prediction-error minimization (Rao & Ballard 1999); neuromorphic hardware (TrueNorth, Loihi) bets on spikes for efficiency; and whether brains approximate backprop remains genuinely open research.

example.code:
from brian2 import *

# Leaky integrate-and-fire: the workhorse neuron model.
tau = 10*ms
eqs = '''
dv/dt = (I - v)/tau : 1
I : 1
'''
G = NeuronGroup(5, eqs, threshold='v>1', reset='v=0', method='exact')
G.I = [0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0]  # drive each neuron differently

spikemon = SpikeMonitor(G)
statemon = StateMonitor(G, 'v', record=True)
run(100*ms)

print('spike counts:', spikemon.count[:])
# Neuron 0 (I=0.8): steady state v=0.8 < threshold 1 -> never spikes.
# Neurons 1-4: steady state above threshold -> regular spiking,
# faster for larger I. Rheobase, demonstrated, not asserted.
example.walkthrough: This is a complete Brian2 experiment in fifteen lines: the equations string declares the LIF dynamics, NeuronGroup instantiates five neurons with different drive currents, and the monitors record spikes and voltage traces. The predicted outcome is the lesson — neuron 0 sits below rheobase (steady state 0.8 < threshold 1) and stays silent while the others fire at rates ordered by their input current. Running it turns the steady-state calculation from scenario 2 into observed data, and the same pattern (equations, monitors, run) scales to the spiking-network capstone.

pitfalls: Common trap: collapsing analogy levels — claiming transformer attention IS biological attention because both 'select information.' Label function vs mechanism every time.
Common trap: simulating before steady-state analysis — compute rheobase and fixed points first; most 'broken' neuron simulations are parameter facts.
Common trap: running unconstrained Hebbian plasticity and calling the explosion a bug — positive feedback without normalization diverges by design.
Common trap: teaching the backprop-in-the-brain question as settled — the weight-transport problem and its proposed alternatives make it open research.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Leaky integrate-and-fire: find the rheobase
labs.objective: Simulate LIF neurons in Brian2 across a sweep of input currents, measure spike counts, and locate the rheobase — the minimum current that produces spiking — comparing it against the analytic steady-state prediction.
steps: Create lab1.py with the lesson's Brian2 LIF snippet, extended to 11 neurons with input currents from 0.5 to 2.5 in steps of 0.2.
Run 200 ms of simulated time, record spike counts per neuron with SpikeMonitor, and print a table of current vs spike count.
Compute the analytic prediction: steady-state v = I (in these units), so rheobase is the current where v crosses threshold 1.0 — print the predicted rheobase.
Compare: identify the first current in your table with nonzero spikes and state whether it matches the prediction, and why boundary cases may differ by one step.
In three sentences, explain what rheobase means biophysically and why a network modeler needs it before wiring neurons together.

checks.hint: Print a line like 'predicted rheobase 1.0 / observed first spiking current 1.1' so the check can see the comparison.

labs.title: Hopfield associative memory in numpy
labs.objective: Implement a Hopfield network with the Hebbian outer-product rule, store a few patterns, corrupt one, and watch the dynamics converge back — then overload it to observe the capacity failure from scenario 4.
steps: Create lab2.py: define 3 random bipolar (+1/-1) patterns of length 100, build the weight matrix as the sum of outer products with zero diagonal, divided by N.
Implement asynchronous updates (random neuron order, sign activation) and an energy function E = -0.5 * s^T W s; verify energy never increases across updates.
Corrupt one pattern by flipping 20 bits, run the dynamics to convergence, and print the overlap (fraction of matching bits) with the original — it should recover fully.
Now store 40 patterns in the same 100 neurons, corrupt one, and run retrieval: print the final overlap and note the spurious-mixture failure.
In three sentences, connect the two runs to the 0.14N capacity result and to the idea of memories as attractors in an energy landscape.

checks.hint: Print lines like 'clean recall overlap 1.0000 / overloaded overlap 0.XXXX' so the check can see both regimes.

simulations.title: The spiking net that won't spike
simulations.brief: The spiking neural network trains for hours and the output layer never fires a single spike. The network is effectively dead.

steps.symptom: Zero spikes at the output layer across all timesteps; loss never moves.
evidence: Peak membrane potential reaches 0.6; firing threshold is set to 2.0
Rate-encoded inputs deliver mean current 0.5 per timestep
tau_mem is 5ms with 100 timesteps — the membrane decays between sparse inputs
options: Lower the firing threshold toward the observed potential range and strengthen the input current
Increase the threshold to 5.0 to make spikes more selective
Add more layers — depth will amplify the signal
Switch to a longer simulation with the same parameters
steps.explain: The membrane never reaches threshold: 0.6 peak against a 2.0 threshold means no neuron can ever fire, so no gradient ever flows. Raising the threshold or adding layers deepens the silence. Bring the threshold into the range the inputs can actually reach.

simulations.debrief: A spiking net that cannot spike cannot learn. Always verify the spike budget first: membrane potentials must actually cross threshold under your inputs, or the whole network is decoration.

simulations.title: Catastrophic forgetting
simulations.brief: The continual-learning agent masters the new navigation task at 90% — and its accuracy on the old grasping task collapses from 88% to 12%.

steps.symptom: New task 90%, old task 12% after sequential training.
evidence: Pure sequential: task B trained with task A data deleted
Synapses critical to task A moved 4x more than average during task B
options: Add experience replay of task A and consolidate important synapses (e.g. elastic weight consolidation)
Train task B longer until task A recovers on its own
Freeze the entire network and only train a new output head
Accept the forgetting — continual learning always loses the old task
steps.explain: Sequential training without replay overwrites the weights task A needs — the weight drift data proves it. Replay keeps old-task gradients alive; consolidation protects the synapses that mattered. More task-B training just digs the hole deeper.

simulations.debrief: Brains do not delete the past to learn the present: replay and consolidation are how continual learners keep old skills. Measure old-task accuracy during new-task training — forgetting is a metric, not a mystery.

simulations.title: Pick the brain-inspired model
simulations.brief: You have event-camera data — sparse, asynchronous brightness changes — for gesture recognition on a neuromorphic chip. Choose the model.

steps.text: Sparse event-camera stream, neuromorphic chip target. Model?

choices.label: Spiking neural network that consumes the event stream natively
choices.feedback: Correct: the data is already spikes. An SNN processes events as they arrive with no frame conversion, matching the chip's asynchronous hardware.

choices.label: Convert events to 60fps frames and run a standard CNN
choices.feedback: Framing the events throws away the temporal sparsity that makes event cameras efficient, then runs a dense CNN on mostly-empty frames — the worst of both worlds.

simulations.debrief: Match the model to the signal: event data wants event-driven models. Converting sparse asynchronous data into dense frames discards exactly the efficiency neuromorphic hardware is built for.

simulations.title: Run the neuromorphic experiment
simulations.brief: Put the neuromorphic experiment steps in the order that produces a trustworthy result.

items: Simulate the SNN and record spike trains
Encode the dataset into spike trains
Compare against the ANN baseline on accuracy and energy
Decode the output spikes into predictions
Measure spike rates and energy per inference

simulations.debrief: Encode first (the encoding is part of the model), simulate and measure spikes, decode to predictions, then compare against the baseline on both accuracy and energy. An SNN that is less accurate and no more efficient than the ANN is a failed experiment.

simulations.title: Review the SNN config
simulations.brief: This spiking network config is headed to the neuromorphic chip. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).

steps.config:
neurons: 1024
threshold: 5.0
tau_mem: 0ms
timesteps: 100
encoding: rate
learning: stdp

issues.description: Threshold 5.0 with the observed input range — neurons will never reach it and the network stays silent.
issues.fix: Set the threshold within the range inputs can reach (e.g. near 1.0).

issues.description: tau_mem of 0ms means the membrane has no memory — it resets instantly and integrates nothing across timesteps.
issues.fix: Set tau_mem to a positive value (e.g. 20ms) so potentials accumulate.

simulations.debrief: SNN configs live or die on neuron dynamics: a reachable threshold and a real membrane time constant. Zero memory plus an unreachable threshold is a network that cannot compute.

behavioral.prompt: Explain the difference between rate coding and temporal coding to an ML engineer who has never studied neuroscience.
points: Start from their world: firing rate as a ReLU-like activation
Introduce timing with one concrete mechanism (STDP)
Name what each code can and cannot express
Connect to a modeling choice they might actually make

Explain what the evidence actually supports

No proposal for how to decide later

cheatsheet: Coding question first: rate vs temporal decides which mechanisms your model can express.
LIF steady state: v_inf = V_rest + R_m * I — compute rheobase before simulating.
Hodgkin-Huxley 1952: squid giant axon, Na+/K+ conductances, gating variables m, h, n.
Hebb 1949: fire together, wire together — plus a stabilizer (Oja, BCM, normalization), always.
STDP: pre-before-post (tens of ms) → strengthen; post-before-pre → weaken (Bi & Poo 1998).
Hopfield: patterns as attractors, energy E = -0.5 s^T W s, capacity ~0.14N.
Analogies carry level labels: function vs mechanism — never collapse them.
Backprop in the brain: open research (weight transport; feedback alignment; predictive coding).
glossary: neural coding
How neurons represent information: rate codes (spike counts) vs temporal codes (timing, latency, synchrony).
leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF)
Neuron model integrating input with leak toward rest; spikes at threshold, then resets.
rheobase
Minimum sustained input current that drives a neuron to spike threshold.
Hodgkin-Huxley model
1952 conductance-based model of the action potential (squid giant axon); Na+/K+ gating variables m, h, n.
action potential
The spike: rapid depolarization, repolarization, and refractory period of the membrane voltage.
refractory period
Brief window after a spike when the neuron cannot (absolute) or hardly can (relative) fire again.
Hebbian plasticity
Hebb 1949: synapses strengthen with correlated pre/post activity — unstable without constraints.
STDP
Spike-timing-dependent plasticity: pre-before-post strengthens, post-before-pre weakens, within tens of ms.
LTP / LTD
Long-term potentiation/depression: lasting increases/decreases in synaptic strength.
Oja's rule / BCM
Hebbian variants with normalization (Oja) or a sliding modification threshold (BCM) for stability.
Hopfield network
Recurrent associative memory (1982): stored patterns as attractors of an energy landscape.
attractor
A stable state (or set) the network dynamics converge to from nearby initial conditions.
NEURON
Yale simulator for detailed compartmental biophysical neuron models (Hines).
Brian2
Python spiking-neural-network simulator using equations strings; the lab instrument of this track.
neuromorphic hardware
Chips computing with spikes and colocalized memory (e.g. IBM TrueNorth, Intel Loihi) for efficiency.
predictive coding
Theory of cortex as hierarchical prediction-error minimization (Rao & Ballard 1999); related to Friston's free-energy principle.
Bayesian brain
The hypothesis that neural computation approximates Bayesian inference under uncertainty.
weight transport problem
Backprop's need for feedback weights mirroring feedforward weights — no clear biological implementation.
feedback alignment
Lillicrap et al. 2016: random fixed feedback weights can still drive useful learning — a candidate alternative.
biological attention
Neuromodulatory and thalamocortical selection mechanisms — functionally akin to, mechanistically distinct from transformer attention.
checklist: Coding assumption stated: rate, temporal, or hybrid — and why the task needs it.
Steady-state / rheobase analysis done before any neuron simulation.
Plasticity rule paired with its stabilizer (normalization, bounds, BCM/Oja).
Hopfield pattern count checked against ~0.14N capacity before debugging retrieval.
Every brain-AI analogy labeled: functional similarity vs mechanistic claim.
Simulation validated against an analytic prediction, with limits documented.
Neuromorphic claims scoped to efficiency/architecture, not cognition.
Open questions (backprop, coding) reported as open — no verdicts taught as fact.

chat.persona: You are a rigorous but encouraging NeuroAI tutor. Teach from first principles, show short real code (Brian2, numpy) when it clarifies, label every brain-AI analogy with its level (function vs mechanism), and treat open research questions as open — never teach a verdict. Stay on topic: neural coding, biophysical neuron models, plasticity, Hopfield networks, spiking simulation, predictive coding, neuromorphic hardware, and the backprop question. Independent study material; no vendor affiliation, no certificates, no medical content.
